title: Linguistic diversity and multilingual repertoires
subtitle: Understanding how languages are acquired, distributed and used in everyday life.

sections.heading: Language and its modalities
paragraphs: Language is a conventional system of signs and patterned relationships through which people communicate, think and participate in social life. Speech is one way of producing language, but it is not the definition of language itself. Natural signed languages have linguistic organization and support complex communication. Writing represents language through a learned visual system. Consequently, a definition requiring every language to be vocal excludes genuine languages and should be corrected.

Monolingualism generally concerns one language, bilingualism two, and multilingualism more than one. Some classroom classifications use multilingualism more narrowly for three or more languages. These conventions should be stated rather than treated as contradictory facts. Trilingualism specifies three. Individual multilingualism concerns a person's repertoire, while societal multilingualism concerns language diversity in a community; a multilingual country need not have only multilingual individuals.

sections.heading: Acquisition and proficiency
paragraphs: Simultaneous acquisition involves early overlapping development, often from infancy. Sequential, successive and consecutive acquisition commonly describe an additional language beginning after earlier language development has started. Receptive bilingualism is different: it describes understanding relative to production, not the age sequence of acquisition. A child may therefore acquire English sequentially and also have stronger receptive than expressive Punjabi. Early and late are useful descriptive labels only when the exposure history and classification are clear.

Balanced proficiency means relative comparability on specified measures, not perfect mastery of every possible topic. Dominance can differ across activities. A learner may read English more confidently but discuss family matters more precisely in Urdu. The first language is not necessarily the currently strongest language. The historical label semilingualism should not replace investigation of specific skills, opportunities and needs. The handout's listed competencies are more usefully assessed individually than treated as evidence of a deficient person.

sections.heading: Domains, vocabulary and literacy
paragraphs: Languages are often developed for complementary purposes. A student may use English for academic reading, Urdu in a city workplace and Punjabi in family conversation. The resulting distribution of knowledge is expected rather than evidence that each language has failed. An unfamiliar school-language label does not prove absence of the underlying concept. Assessment must investigate the relevant language resources and experiences instead of imagining a bilingual as two identical monolinguals.

Biliteracy concerns reading and writing in two languages and does not follow automatically from speaking them. Similarly, knowledge of two spoken languages is commonly called unimodal bilingualism, while use of a signed and a spoken language can be bimodal. A complete language history records acquisition, exposure, communication partners, domains, schooling, modalities and changes over time. A binary bilingual label alone cannot provide that information.

sections.heading: Maintenance, addition and loss
paragraphs: Additive bilingual development supports an additional language while maintaining the earlier language. It does not require equal test scores. Subtractive conditions involve erosion of the earlier language's opportunities or development, often where a dominant language gains social or institutional power. Learning another language is not inherently subtractive. Meaningful family interaction, community opportunities and literacy resources can support maintenance.

Language shift concerns changing community or family patterns of use, often across generations. Attrition concerns reduced accessibility or proficiency and can affect particular resources rather than erase an entire language. A heritage language can remain personally important even when literacy or production is less developed. Migration and school arrangements influence these patterns, but no single family strategy guarantees a particular result.

sections.heading: Contact and flexible use
paragraphs: Code-switching involves alternation between languages or varieties; code-mixing often refers to combining elements within an utterance. Authors draw these boundaries differently, so examples should be described before labels are imposed. A technical English noun in an Urdu sentence may be a bilingual insertion or an established loanword; community distribution and conventionalization help distinguish the possibilities. Neither observation alone diagnoses confusion.

Translanguaging emphasizes how people draw on a multilingual repertoire to make meaning. It can support learning while teachers still explain audience expectations and particular language conventions. Cross-linguistic influence can help or complicate performance, depending on the feature and task. It should not be equated automatically with impairment.

sections.heading: Benefits and careful conclusions
paragraphs: Additional languages can widen relationships, access and participation. Metalinguistic awareness concerns reflection on language forms and meanings, such as noticing that two words can name the same object. Claims that bilingualism universally improves intelligence, reasoning or executive function are stronger than the evidence warrants. Results vary across tasks, populations and study conditions, and publication bias complicates broad conclusions.

The deck's precise worldwide percentages should not be memorized as established facts without a clearly defined population, measure and source. A hypothetical English-Mandarin-Cantonese household illustrates opportunities for trilingual development, not a guaranteed outcome from hearing three languages. For exam reasoning, describe the actual repertoire, distinguish age of acquisition from proficiency, and avoid turning a useful social benefit into an unsupported universal prediction.

title: Bilingual development, assessment and intervention
subtitle: Distinguishing difference from disorder and planning useful support across languages.

sections.heading: Understanding the lecture's myths
paragraphs: Bilingualism does not itself constitute a communication disorder. Equal ability in both languages is not required, and childhood is not the only possible period for becoming bilingual. Mixed utterances can be normal resources in communication. These principles correct several common assumptions in the lecture's true-or-false prompts. They do not mean that bilingual children cannot have disorders; they mean that concerns require appropriate investigation rather than explanation through bilingual status alone.

One-person-one-language is one possible family arrangement. It is neither mandatory nor a guarantee of balanced proficiency. A family may use its heritage language at home, vary languages by activity or draw flexibly on shared resources. The relevant question is whether children have meaningful, accessible opportunities to communicate, not whether the family follows one supposedly universal formula.

sections.heading: Language access and family decisions
paragraphs: A blanket recommendation to stop the home language can disrupt valued communication without addressing the actual difficulty. Families should be supported in using languages through which they can interact meaningfully and comfortably. School placement, optional enrichment and therapy arrangements can be reconsidered when necessary, but decisions should be collaborative and individualized. Neither a fixed exposure percentage nor a claim of inevitable permanent damage provides an adequate decision rule.

A child may understand a home language well while answering in the school language. The difference could reflect practice, preference, audience or proficiency. Language history should therefore explore when each language began, who uses it, how frequently meaningful interactions occur, and what the child needs to communicate. Hearing access, development and family concerns also belong in the assessment picture.

sections.heading: Difference, disorder and learning
paragraphs: A language difference is a pattern explained by linguistic background or learning experience rather than impairment. A language disorder concerns difficulties that are not adequately explained solely by opportunity to learn a particular language. Manifestations can differ across languages; clinicians should not demand identical errors everywhere or diagnose from a single unfamiliar-language score. Persistent concerns across the repertoire require informed evaluation, not automatic reassurance.

Language samples reveal communication during conversation, narratives and other relevant tasks. Dynamic assessment examines how performance changes with supported teaching, often through test-teach-retest procedures. Modifiability concerns responsiveness and the effort required for learning. Rapid learning is useful information, but no one observation independently excludes every possible disorder. Interpret the evidence together with history, appropriate measures and functional observations.

sections.heading: Vocabulary measurement
paragraphs: Single-language vocabulary scores can underestimate distributed knowledge. Total vocabulary counts known word forms across languages, while conceptual vocabulary counts each underlying concept once. If a child knows thirty Urdu labels and twenty English labels, with twelve translation-equivalent pairs, the total is fifty word forms but thirty-eight distinct concepts. The subtraction removes duplicated concepts, not evidence of learning.

These counts do not automatically produce valid standardized scores. A clinician must check the inventory, scoring convention and suitability of comparison data. Translating a published English test changes item and administration properties; original norms are not automatically preserved. When standardized interpretation is unsupported, document what was done and describe performance appropriately rather than presenting invented normative precision.

sections.heading: Intervention targets and transfer
paragraphs: A bilingual approach can address shared skills or features, such as useful narrative organization. A cross-linguistic approach also attends to language-specific needs and contrasts. The distinction does not imply choosing only one language forever. Consider the person's communication priorities, linguistic systems and available expertise. An SLP can collaborate with qualified language support when the client's language differs from the clinician's.

The instruction to teach structure rather than vocabulary should be read critically. Concepts, useful labels and sentence structures can support one another. A child might learn words for school materials within functional request patterns, then use them with relevant partners. Stories and pictures can help, but their content and conventions must be familiar or explained; they are not automatically culturally universal.

sections.heading: Monitoring and collaboration
paragraphs: Collect baseline information and plan repeated probes. Separate success on practiced items from generalization to new items, settings or languages. Improvement after Urdu practice does not establish improvement in English unless relevant English performance is checked. Functional participation matters alongside structured targets: communicating with grandparents, asking a teacher for help and repairing a misunderstanding may be meaningful outcomes.

Caregiver coaching should fit family routines, literacy, language access and time. Homework difficulties should prompt discussion of barriers rather than judgments about commitment. An interpreter supports spoken or signed exchanges; a translator works with written material; a cultural broker can help clarify relevant meanings. These roles support the clinician's work without transferring away clinical responsibility. Finally, accommodation can mean improving access, while assimilation can mean adoption of dominant practices. Piagetian assimilation and accommodation refer instead to using or modifying cognitive schemes. Context determines which meaning is intended.

title: Second-language learning and proficiency models
subtitle: Using acquisition stages and Cummins’s distinctions without turning them into rigid rules.

sections.heading: Acquisition as a variable process
paragraphs: Additional-language learning develops through interaction among prior knowledge, meaningful exposure, opportunities to participate, instruction and personal circumstances. Learners can show different abilities in listening, speaking, reading, writing or signing. They can also perform differently across familiar and unfamiliar situations. A stage description is therefore a broad teaching guide rather than a complete psychological profile.

The lecture names pre-production, early production, speech emergence, intermediate fluency and advanced fluency. These descriptions help teachers consider suitable support, but fixed vocabulary totals and six-month intervals should not be treated as individual diagnostic rules. Progress can vary across tasks and periods of changing opportunity. A learner may produce a complex rehearsed phrase while finding a simpler unfamiliar exchange difficult.

sections.heading: Early participation and increasing production
paragraphs: Pre-production describes limited overt output in a new language. The learner may still understand routines, follow gestures and communicate nonverbally. A silent period does not mean absence of thought or absence of language in the home setting. Neither should it justify ignoring concerns indefinitely. Consider exposure, comprehension, participation, anxiety and the broader developmental profile when deciding whether further evaluation is needed.

Early production often involves brief responses. Speech emergence describes increasing phrases and simple sentences with continuing errors. Intermediate fluency allows more complex participation while clarification and explicit support can remain important. Advanced fluency likewise does not mean complete knowledge of every discipline or genre. All learners continue encountering unfamiliar words, communicative expectations and specialized writing demands.

sections.heading: Conversational and academic proficiency
paragraphs: Cummins's BICS/CALP distinction draws attention to differences between everyday conversational proficiency and the language demands of academic learning. BICS is commonly discussed through familiar interpersonal exchanges supported by shared context. CALP highlights language needed for curriculum reasoning and academic literacy. These are conceptual distinctions about proficiency and demands, not two separate organs or two wholly independent languages.

A child may chat easily with friends but struggle to write an explanation of a scientific process. The task can require precise vocabulary, explicit causal relationships and unfamiliar genre conventions. Conversational success therefore does not prove readiness for every academic task, and difficulty with the report does not by itself prove low intelligence or language disorder. Ask what linguistic and conceptual work the task actually requires.

sections.heading: Context and cognitive demand
paragraphs: Contextual support includes demonstrations, gestures, pictures, shared objects and opportunities to clarify. Context-reduced communication offers fewer immediate supports, although background knowledge and accompanying resources can still help. Cognitive demand concerns the reasoning and conceptual work involved. These dimensions are related in experience but analytically distinct.

Explaining competing predictions during a visible experiment can be cognitively demanding and context-embedded. Copying a familiar expression can be relatively undemanding despite limited visual support. The instructional aim need not be to remove intellectual challenge when language access is difficult. A teacher can preserve complex thinking while adding demonstrations, structured discussion and vocabulary support.

sections.heading: Shared resources and transfer
paragraphs: Common Underlying Proficiency proposes that some knowledge and skills can support performance across languages. The iceberg image illustrates different visible surface forms above a shared base. It is a metaphor, not a literal brain diagram or proof that every linguistic structure transfers automatically. Knowing how to organize an explanation in Urdu can help, while English expressions still require opportunities to learn and use them.

Transfer depends on what is shared, what differs and how instruction connects the resources. A learner who understands farming processes may need labels rather than entirely new concepts. Conversely, familiar vocabulary does not ensure understanding of an unfamiliar scientific relationship. Distinguish underlying knowledge from the language through which it is currently demonstrated.

sections.heading: Supporting learning and interpreting benefits
paragraphs: Scaffolding provides temporary support adjusted toward independence. A teacher can model an explanation, guide attempts and gradually reduce prompts. Meaningful interaction permits learners to negotiate understanding, request clarification and respond to feedback. Wait time recognizes processing and formulation demands. Pictures should be checked for relevance rather than assumed to be universally transparent.

Academic vocabulary, disciplinary genres, narrative conventions, inference and synthesis deserve explicit attention. Formative assessment can identify whether a learner needs conceptual explanation, linguistic support or both. Select goals from observed communication needs rather than elapsed time alone. The lecture's benefits list should also be interpreted carefully: multilingual experience can widen participation and identity resources, but it does not guarantee greater creativity, self-esteem or executive performance for every person. Evidence should be tied to the particular outcome measured and the context in which it was studied.

title: Culture, language and intercultural communication
subtitle: Understanding patterned meanings while respecting individual variation.

sections.heading: Culture as learned and changing practice
paragraphs: Culture concerns learned patterns of meanings, values, practices and social organization. An idealist emphasis foregrounds beliefs and ideas, a materialist emphasis attends to observable practice and material conditions, and an omnibus definition includes several dimensions. These are analytic emphases rather than three separate kinds of people. Anthropology studies human life across contexts, while linguistic anthropology examines how language participates in social and cultural activity.

Culture changes and overlaps. Nationality, religion, ethnicity, racialization, language and socioeconomic position can matter, but none supplies a complete account of one person's experience. Two families who share a language may prefer different interaction styles. Cultural identity can involve multiple affiliations. Asking about the actual person's preferences is more reliable than treating a regional or religious label as a behavioral instruction manual.

sections.heading: Language, signs and cultural meanings
paragraphs: Language helps express, maintain and negotiate cultural meanings. Kinship terms, greetings, proverbs and choices of address can communicate social relationships. This does not establish that each culture has exactly one language or that one language represents only one culture. Multilingual communities and shared languages across different communities make the relationship more complex.

Arbitrariness describes the conventional relationship between many forms and meanings. It does not mean that language use is randomly improvised without shared rules. Meaningful structure, duality of patterning and productivity describe how patterned resources support meaningful combinations and novel expression. Language also changes through ordinary use and contact. Signed languages demonstrate why these properties should not be restricted to vocal communication alone.

sections.heading: Development and social participation
paragraphs: Children learn language through experience and participation. Perceptual tuning during infancy reflects exposure-related changes in sensitivity to speech contrasts; it is not an abrupt universal switch on one birthday. Early vocabulary varies, and multilingual knowledge can be distributed across languages. Assess appropriate developmental information rather than diagnosing from one narrow word-count statement.

Telegraphic speech describes early combinations that often emphasize content words while omitting some grammatical elements. Many children begin word combinations around age two, so the slide's thirty-month statement should not become a universal onset rule. Language growth continues through schooling and beyond, including discourse and specialized vocabulary. A fixed claim that every child learns thirteen words daily is not an individual milestone.

sections.heading: Social variation without deficit assumptions
paragraphs: Sociolinguistics examines language in social life. Age, networks, education, gender, social class and ethnic identification can be associated with patterns of use. They do not establish universal behavior or the grammatical superiority of privileged groups. Statements that women naturally use more sophisticated language or that working-class speakers possess simpler systems should be replaced with context-sensitive investigation.

African American English illustrates systematic variation rather than defective English. Some varieties have negative concord or context-governed copula absence. These patterns require knowledge of their distribution; they do not license arbitrary omission in every grammatical environment. A school writing convention can differ from a child's community grammar without turning that grammar into a clinical disorder.

sections.heading: Taboo, indirectness and interpretation
paragraphs: A taboo concerns socially regulated sensitivities or prohibitions. Linguistic taboos concern expressions or ways of referring to a subject. A euphemism offers less direct or more acceptable reference, while a dysphemism deliberately makes reference harsher. Their effect depends on participants and context; a supposedly polite substitute can also obscure important meaning.

Idioms have conventional meanings not fully predictable word by word. Proverbs communicate general observations or advice. Humor often depends on shared knowledge and expectations. Difficulty with an unfamiliar joke does not independently diagnose disorder. The lecture's examples of gaze, food, personal space and religious practices should prompt respectful inquiry, not assumptions that every individual follows one fixed rule.

sections.heading: Intercultural and clinical communication
paragraphs: Intercultural communication involves interpretation across differing experiences and meaning systems. Grammatical proficiency is useful but insufficient when participants understand gestures, indirect requests or politeness differently. Nonverbal resources include gaze, posture, facial expression and distance. Proxemics concerns spatial behavior. Ask whether seating and interaction are comfortable rather than assigning one universal distance or gaze requirement.

Cultural humility involves continuing reflection on assumptions and openness to learning from others. Cultural responsiveness applies relevant information to communication and services. Ethnocentrism treats one's own habits as the unquestioned standard; stereotypes replace individual evidence with group generalizations. An SLP can instead explain a task, invite correction, check understanding and adapt materials while preserving the intended assessment or learning aim. Respectful clarification supports accurate interpretation and better participation without requiring anyone to represent an entire community.

title: Dialects, social variation and regional diversity
subtitle: Describing language varieties without confusing social status with linguistic ability.

sections.heading: Dialect, accent and variety
paragraphs: A dialect is a systematic regional or social variety that can differ in pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar and patterns of use. Accent is narrower: it concerns pronunciation. All speakers use varieties, including institutionally supported standard dialects. The word variety is useful when the question concerns a region, social group, activity or individual pattern without assuming one rigid language boundary.

Regional dialects are associated with places, sociolects with social groups, and idiolects with individual patterns. Regiolect and topolect are geographically oriented labels used in particular traditions. Voice quality and temporary physical state can make a speaker recognizable, but a hoarse voice is not itself a new dialect. Social networks and communities of practice help explain how speakers acquire and maintain ways of speaking through relationships and shared activities.

sections.heading: Standards, prestige and choice
paragraphs: A standard variety receives institutional support, often through education, publication and codification. Standardization can involve selecting forms, codifying conventions, expanding functions and gaining acceptance. None of these processes creates grammar where no linguistic system previously existed. Nonstandard varieties are systematic even when institutions value them differently.

Overt prestige concerns explicitly approved forms. Covert prestige concerns positive local meanings attached to forms that may be stigmatized elsewhere. A speaker can value local solidarity and also learn institutional writing conventions. Bidialectal development can expand choices without requiring rejection of a home variety. Discrimination arises when social judgments about accents or dialects substitute for relevant evidence about an individual's abilities.

sections.heading: Situation and interaction
paragraphs: Register varies with activity and purpose, such as technical discussion among clinicians or accessible explanation to a family. Jargon is specialized group vocabulary. Style shifting allows speakers to adjust forms for different audiences and settings. Communication accommodation theory includes convergence toward another person's patterns and divergence that emphasizes distinctiveness.

These adjustments need not involve permanent loss of identity. A local feature can express affiliation in one setting and be reduced in another. Age differences also need careful interpretation. A feature common among teenagers might reflect life-stage practices, generational change or other circumstances. Historical comparison or following cohorts over time helps distinguish these possibilities.

sections.heading: Boundaries and classifications
paragraphs: Mutual intelligibility concerns understanding between users of varieties. It is informative but not a complete rule for language status. Exposure, asymmetrical comprehension, political histories and speaker identities complicate classification. A dialect continuum can show relatively small differences between neighbors but substantial differences across the wider region. An isogloss maps a particular feature's distribution; different features need not share the same boundary.

The lecture's seven criteria are standardization, vitality, historicity, autonomy, reduction, mixture and de facto norms. They are discussion tools, not a mechanical score deciding human worth or linguistic legitimacy. Vitality concerns active use and transmission; historicity concerns historical identity; autonomy concerns perceived independence. Functional restriction and contact history do not make speakers intellectually deficient. De facto norms can operate without official grammars or written policies.

sections.heading: Punjab and adjoining regional labels
paragraphs: The supplied deck lists Shahpuri, Jhangochi or Jhangvi, Jangli or Rachnavi, Malwai, Doabi, Pothwari, Derawali, Hindko, Thali and Chenavari. They are important course terms, but the slide's broad Punjabi grouping should not be treated as an uncontested modern taxonomy. Shahpuri is associated with the Shahpur-Sargodha area; Jhangochi with Jhang and adjoining speech; Rachnavi labels relate to the Rachna Doab. Claims that one variety is the oldest require evidence beyond a teaching slide.

Malwai is especially associated with Malwa in Indian Punjab; Doabi is historically associated with the area between the Beas and Sutlej. Migration carries varieties beyond historical regions. Pahari-Pothwari classifications vary across sources and communities. Derawali is often considered within Saraiki-related descriptions, while Hindko has its own language identities and regional distinctions. Thali and Chenavari labels require attention to local use and source-specific classification. Majhi provides an additional central-Punjab reference without making other varieties less legitimate.

sections.heading: Implications for SLP and education
paragraphs: Record how clients identify their languages and investigate relevant linguistic features. A clinician should not override a family's Hindko, Saraiki or Pothwari identification merely because a slide uses a broader label. Precise borders, mixture claims and historical priorities should be verified through appropriate regional work rather than memorized as settled facts.

Dialect-informed assessment distinguishes community-appropriate forms from impairment using the person's history, relevant linguistic information and multiple measures. Teaching a standard convention may be useful for a particular educational goal, but it is a different act from diagnosing disorder. Language policy, whether written or implicit, influences access. Revitalization can support transmission and meaningful use where opportunities decline. The practical principle throughout is to describe the actual pattern and its context before assigning a social judgment or clinical conclusion.
